query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy based on HfMoTaTiZr modified with a minor Cr addition (approximately 4.2 at% Cr, as in HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5) will perform better as a protective material for hot‐dip aluminum plating equipment because the Cr addition promotes the formation of small, dispersed Laves phase precipitates within a strong BCC matrix. This dual-phase microstructure enhances high‐temperature strength and ductility, imparting improved resistance to molten aluminum erosion.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast HfMoTaTiZr refractory HEA that is initially in a single-phase BCC state.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of about 4.2 at% Cr into the base HfMoTaTiZr alloy to induce a controlled precipitation of a Cr-rich Laves phase in addition to the BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature liquid aluminum during hot-dip plating, where components are in long-term contact with molten aluminum.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a minor, evenly distributed Laves phase (Cr-rich intermetallic) within the continuous BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The Cr addition increases lattice distortion and promotes precipitation of a Laves phase that acts as a barrier to crack propagation and aluminum dissolution. Simultaneously, the enhanced yield strength and improved ductility of the dual-phase microstructure can better withstand thermal and mechanical stresses in the corrosive environment of molten aluminum.
generation.predicted_outcome: Parts fabricated from the Cr-modified refractory HEA are expected to exhibit lower erosion rates, reduced weight loss, and maintain mechanical integrity for longer service life compared to parts made from the unmodified single-phase alloy.
generation.baseline: Unmodified HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a single-phase BCC structure, which may suffer faster degradation under molten aluminum exposure due to lower high-temperature strength and lack of a protective secondary phase.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is anticipated only under conditions where the operating temperature and exposure time remain within the stability range of the dual-phase microstructure; unforeseen reactive interactions with molten aluminum or excessively long exposures may still lead to degradation.
generation.uncertainty: While enhanced mechanical properties and phase stability in HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 are documented, its direct corrosion resistance against molten aluminum has not been explicitly measured. The actual interfacial reaction kinetics and long-term chemical compatibility with liquid aluminum remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of dipping and plating equipment parts: one set fabricated from the unmodified HfMoTaTiZr alloy and the other from the Cr-modified HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 alloy. Subject both sets to prolonged exposure in a molten aluminum bath at typical hot-dip plating temperatures (e.g., around 660°C or slightly higher) for an extended period while monitoring weight loss, surface degradation, and mechanical integrity. Post-exposure, analyze the microstructure using SEM and XRD.
measurements: Surface morphology and extent of erosion (via SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-modified alloy does not show statistically significant improvement in terms of lower weight loss, reduced surface degradation, and better retention of mechanical properties compared to the unmodified alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s).
